replies:
Okay — I'll mock you now. I'll ask the first interview question for a financial analyst role; answer as you would in the room (type your full answer). I'll score it for structure, evidence and specificity, give one concrete improvement, then ask the next question.

Here's the first question:
"Tell me about a time you identified a financial process or model that was producing misleading results. What did you do, and what was the outcome?"

Structure: 1/3 — you named the action but not the situation or result. Evidence: 0/3 — no metrics, no tools, no role. Specificity: 1/3 — say which model, which comps, timeline, your role.

One concrete improvement: give Situation -> Task -> Action -> Result, add a numeric result (time saved, error reduced, forecast accuracy improved) or say you couldn't measure and why.

I'll ask the next question now: "Tell me about a time you worked with a team under a deadline."

Saved: Practicing a mock for a financial analyst interview; answered initial question with approach to build a three-statement model and check against comps. Is that right?

You gave a start but it's weak for an interview.

Score (honest)
- Structure (STAR): 1/3 — you jumped to the action (what you'd do) without setting the Situation or Task, and you gave no Result.
- Evidence: 0/3 — no specifics on what you actually did, what tools/models you used, dates, or your role.
- Specificity: 1/3 — you named a three-statement model and comps, but not which drivers, which comps, timeframe, or measurable impact.
Why this matters (brief): Interviewers need to hear you actually did this — what problem you faced, your exact steps, how you coordinated, and a concrete outcome (numbers or a clear qualitative benefit). Right now it sounds like a generic method, not a proven achievement.
One concrete revision (use STAR + numbers)
- Situation: "At [company/team], our monthly forecast kept missing by ~15% because bookings timing was off."
- Task: "I was asked to find the root cause and fix the forecast within two weeks."
- Action: "I rebuilt the three-statement model (Excel, scenario tabs) from revenue drivers — bookings by channel, ARR churn, average contract value — and reconciled it to GAAP revenue. I then benchmarked assumptions against three public comps (A, B, C) and adjusted seasonality and booking-to-revenue recognition lags. I automated sensitivity tables and added validation checks (variance >5% flags)."
- Result: "Forecast error fell from 15% to 4% over the next two months; month-end close time shortened by 1 day; finance leadership used the model for quarterly planning."

Practice this exact answer now: type a 60–90 second STAR answer using your real company, your title, one comp name (or 'comps' if you can't), and a numeric result or a clear qualitative outcome. I will score it and give one precise tweak. Is it okay to assume you used Excel and compared to three comps?

What to expect (likely)
- Format: 1 interview ~45–60 minutes (could be two shorter ones). Expect a mix: technical modeling/valuation, a short case or transaction discussion, and behavioral fit.
- Interviewers: senior analyst/associate and a more senior banker (VP/director). They’ll test technical accuracy, commercial judgment, attention to detail, and client maturity.

30-minute prep checklist (do these now, in order)
1) Resume-to-story (10 min)
- Prepare a 3-minute walk-through of your resume linking each role to 2 skills they want: modeling, financial analysis, due diligence, and client/stakeholder communication. End with why Lincoln: mid-market M&A exposure and end-to-end deal experience [replace with your real reason].
2) Technical refresh (15–30 min)
- LBO basics: transaction mechanics, sources & uses, leverage effects, and exit math.
- DCF essentials: project unlevered free cash flow, determine terminal value (perpetuity vs exit multiple), and WACC basics (where cost of equity and debt come from).
- Comps and precedent logic: selecting peers, trimming outliers, and translating EV/EBITDA to equity value.
- Quick mental drills: build a 3-statement link (income → working capital → cashflow) and explain a sensitivity table.
3) STAR stories (15–20 min)
- Prepare 5 crisp STARs: teamwork, leading under pressure, catching an error (attention to detail), learning a hard skill (technical), and a weakness + improvement. Keep each 60–90 seconds and end with a quantified result when possible.

4) Deal thinking & questions (10–15 min)
- Pick one sector Lincoln works in that you know (e.g., industrials, healthcare services, tech-enabled services). Prepare 3 bullets: market trend, consolidation dynamics, and margin drivers.
- Prepare 3 questions to ask them: (1) a recent Lincoln deal that interests them and your role there; (2) typical learning path for analysts; (3) how feedback/mentoring works day-to-day.
How to answer the main types of prompts
- Walk me through your resume (30–45s)
  Structure: one-sentence current role + one-sentence prior role → 3 core strengths with a quick example each → why Lincoln. Be specific: tools (Excel modeling, Capital IQ) only if you use them.

- Behavioral (STAR)
  Structure: Situation, Task, Action (exact steps you did), Result (numbers, timeline). Always name who you coordinated with and what you learned.

- Technical short-answer
  Start with the short definition, then 2–3 quick bullets on mechanics, then a 1-sentence example illustrating commercial impact (e.g., how terminal value can dominate).
- Case / buy decision (10–15 min)
  Framework: Market (size/trend), Profitability/margins and drivers, Growth/capex needs, Risks, Quick valuation (EV multiple check) and buyer fit (strategic vs PE). Say the 2-3 additional pieces of info you’d ask for to decide.
Three targeted practice prompts (answer one now; I’ll score and give one fix)
1) Technical: "Explain a DCF and how terminal value can dominate the valuation. What steps do you take to limit that dominance?"
2) Behavioral: "Tell me about a time you found an important error in a model. What did you do and what was the outcome?"
3) Quick case: "You’re looking at a mid-market services company with steady margins and modest growth. Would you buy it? What three financial/market facts do you ask for first, and why?"
Short scripts you can say now (use your facts)
- Quick opening: "I’m currently [title at Company]. I focus on financial modeling, due diligence and supporting deal execution; before that I [prior role]. I’m excited about Lincoln because [one-line reason tied to deal exposure]."
- Behavioral template: "At [Company], we were preparing [project]. I noticed [problem]. I did [actions — recalculated, communicated, updated deliverable], which resulted in [quantified result]. I learned [what you improved]."
Presentation & logistics
- Bring blank paper to sketch models; write legibly. If asked to model live, state assumptions aloud, show logic, and keep the math simple and checkable.
- If given a technical test, narrate your steps, call out common pitfalls, and check your final answer with a quick sanity check (no negative equity, margin in plausible range).
- Follow-up: prepare a 1–2 sentence thank-you referencing a specific technical point or cultural note from the interview to send afterward (you’ll send it yourself).
One next step
Pick one of the three practice prompts above and answer it here now; I’ll score it for structure, evidence and specificity and give one concrete fix, then we’ll run the next prompt.

Saved nothing about you yet. Is that right?

What I will prepare and show you to approve, field by field, for that first application (I assume a standard online employer form and a concise, truthful tone; tell me if you want a different tone):

1) Employer and job link
- The exact title and company and the job URL you chose. Shown so you confirm it's the right posting.
2) Resume file
- A tailored PDF built only from your confirmed facts. If you haven't provided a resume or confirmed facts, the card will prompt you to paste/upload one or set your name and email. I will state the resume filename and give a private review link.

3) Resume persona
- Which persona is used (default: base), and which confirmed facts will lead. I’ll note any facts left out.

4) Full name and contact info
- Name and email exactly as you told me; phone left as [phone] unless you set it. The card prompts to fill any missing contact info.
5) Location / remote preference
- Filled from your confirmed location or left to match the posting (onsite city or remote). If the posting allows remote, I’ll set your chosen preference or leave it for you.

6) Current title / employer (what shows on the application)
- Filled from confirmed facts; if none, left as [current title / employer].

7) Work authorization
- Shown as you confirmed it, or left as [work authorization] for you to enter. I will not guess.

8) Salary expectation
- If the posting lists pay, I copy it exactly. If it asks your expectation and you have a confirmed salary requirement, I use that; otherwise left as [salary expectation] for you to fill.
9) Earliest start date
- Left as [earliest start date] unless you confirm it; I’ll suggest a sensible default (2–4 weeks) unless you say otherwise.

10) Attachments
- The tailored resume, plus any files you confirmed (certificates, transcripts, portfolio link). Missing requested files are shown as [missing].
11) Cover letter / open-text answers
- A short application text (<=400 words) or responses to required fields:
  - 1–2 sentence opening: who you are, current title/location (from confirmed facts), and why you want this role.
  - 2–3 short accomplishment sentences tailored to the posting’s top skills.
  - 1-sentence close with availability and call to action.
  - Any unknown facts remain as [brackets] for you to fill.

12) Screening questions / checkboxes / selects
- Prefilled only when a confirmed fact answers them (e.g., yes to willingness to relocate only if you confirmed that). Otherwise left blank for you to confirm.
13) Linked profiles and portfolio URLs
- Included only if you provided exact links in confirmed facts; otherwise left blank.

14) References
- Not added unless you provide confirmed reference names. I may include “References available upon request” where appropriate.

15) Diversity / voluntary fields
- Left as the employer default (usually optional); I will not answer without your instruction.

16) Assessments / pre-hire tests
- If present, I’ll note the test link and any deadline on the card; I cannot take tests for you.

17) Background-check / consent statements
- I copy the employer text and leave the required checkbox for you to check in the extension.
18) Final checklist and preview
- Every filled field and every bracketed item shown for you to edit. A checklist of missing items that will block submission (e.g., missing phone, missing authorization, missing file).
- Exact time the application will be queued if you press approve (nothing is sent until you approve it in the extension).

19) Notes to you
- Any flags from the posting (e.g., required certificates, location mismatch, pay not listed) and quick tailoring notes I used (keywords added to resume/cover).
What I assume for this walkthrough: you want a concise, truthful application; standard online form fields; resume built from your confirmed facts. If anything is missing, I leave it bracketed for you to fill before approval.
